newsitem.title: GREECE: Angry farmers extend roadblocks to western Greece.
newsitem.headline: Angry farmers extend roadblocks to western Greece.

text.p: Greece's socialist government faced rising anger against economic austerity on Sunday with farmers expanding a four-day blockade of major highways and an array of other groups planning strikes.
The government appealed on Sunday to farm union leaders to come to Athens for talks but the initial reaction from the farmers was to reject the offer.

"The only movement they're going to see on these highways is hot blood in our veins," one farmer told television reporters after hearing of the government request. Another said: "Every time they talk to us, all they say is more taxes, taxes, taxes."
A motley fleet of some 5,000 farm tractors has seized toll booths and blockaded the main north-south national road as well as rail links throughout the central Thessaly farming region.

Farmers in western Greece joined the protest on Sunday and blockaded the national highway outside the port of Patras with tractors and blazing fires, stopping traffic arriving by ferry from Italy from heading to the Greek capital.

Protests against the 1997 budget submitted on Friday have been growing. Strikes have been called for the coming week by prison wardens, pensioners, teachers, port and tax officials, construction workers and the civil servants union.
Fires burned through the night to stave off cold and rain. Tents were thrown up among the sea of tractors choking Thessaly roads and towns.
Police said there were blockades at some 20 points on roads around Greece. Only army, police or emergency transport could pass the barricades.

The protest has effectively cut land links between Athens and the country's second city, the northern port of Salonika. The north-south land links are the main means of transporting goods and produce between the two cities.

The farmers, many flying black flags or banners proclaiming "Don't Give In" from their tractors, branched out on sideroads between Larissa and Salonika to stop trucks, buses and motorists from skirting the main highway, police said.
Convoys of commercial trucks began to line the highway.
A similar farm protest in March 1995 lasted for 10 days, sent food prices skyrocketing and crippled international road transport.

Farmers want lower fuel costs, a cut in Value Added Tax (VAT) on farm equipment, higher price supports -- especially for cotton -- and rescheduling $1.3 billion in debts owed to the state Agricultural Bank.
Government officials, including Deputy Agriculture Minister Dimitris Sotirlis, went to the centre of the farm rebellion in Larissa and said they were willing to make compromises.
But they said there was no question of squeezing more money out of the 1997 budget for Greek agriculture.

"We have listened to government promises before, especially in 1995. They were never honoured. This time we will block the highway until Christmas. We have nothing to lose," said Mihalis Georgios, a farmers' representative in Larissa.
The 1997 budget set out tough targets to put the economy on track for convergence with Greece's European Union partners by the turn of the century.
Spending was cut, taxes increased and an array of tax exemptions dumped. Greece's largest labour unions held a 24-hour nationwide strike on Thursday to protest against the budget.
